Deutsch-Heft means "German notebook". Lektion 1–18 are reconstructed foundation lessons (your notebook started at 19); Lektion 19–49 are your notebook pages, typed up with the corrections applied, plus the 100-verb list, an exercise sheet, a register of every mistake you make more than once, an ÖSD exam-training section, flashcards for every noun and a quiz that marks itself. Two lessons have no photographed page — 38, and 45, which is rebuilt from the Perfekt lessons either side of it. Articles are coloured the same way as your chart.

Die eine Regel: jedes Nomen groß. (The one rule: every noun capitalised.) Every German noun starts with a capital letter — der Mann, das Mädchen, die Stunde. This was the one mistake on every page, so it's the first thing to drill.

§

Grundbegriffe (basic terms)

What an article is, the four kinds you have learned and how they differ, and the grammar words used in every lesson

Was ist ein Artikel? (What is an article?)

An article is the small word that stands in front of a noun. English has only the and a / an. German articles do more work: they tell you the noun's gender (masculine / feminine / neuter), its number (singular / plural) and its case (nominative / accusative). That is why one English word becomes several German forms.

Bestimmter Artikel (definite article) = "the"
der · die · das · die — for a specific, known thing: the one we already talked about, or the only one there is. Der Mann ist glücklich. (The man is happy.) Die Sonne scheint. (The sun is shining.)
Unbestimmter Artikel (indefinite article) = "a / an"
ein · eine · ein · — — for something new or not specific, one of many. It has no plural. Das ist ein Mann. (This is a man.) Das sind Bücher. (These are books.)
Negativartikel (negative article) = "not a / no"
kein · keine · kein · keine — says a thing is not that noun. It is ein with a k, and unlike ein it does have a plural. Das ist kein Mann. (This is not a man.) Das sind keine Sterne. (These are not stars.)
Possessivartikel (possessive article) = "my, your, his, her …"
mein · meine · mein · meine (and dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr, ihr) — says who owns the noun. Takes exactly the endings of ein / kein. Das ist mein Mann. (This is my husband.)
Die vier Artikel im Vergleich (the four articles side by side · Nominativ)
Artikel (article)Englishmaskulin (m.)feminin (f.)neutral (n.)Plural (pl.)Beispiel (example)
bestimmt (definite)thederdiedasdieder Kuli
unbestimmt (indefinite)a / aneineineein—ein Kuli
negativ (negative)not a / nokeinkeinekeinkeinekein Kuli
possessiv (possessive)my …meinmeinemeinmeinemein Kuli

Der Unterschied (the difference)

  • bestimmt ↔ unbestimmtknown vs new: Das ist ein Kuli. Der Kuli ist rot. — first mention ein, from then on der.
  • unbestimmt ↔ negativein says "yes, it is one"; kein says "no, it is not one". Same endings, plus plural keine.
  • ein-Wörter (ein-words)ein, kein and all the possessives share one ending pattern: nothing for maskulin/neutral, -e for feminin/Plural. Learn the pattern once, use it for all of them.
  • der-Wörter (der-words)der, die, das themselves — the one set that has three different forms in the singular.

Wörter, die in jeder Lektion vorkommen (words that appear in every lesson)

  • das Nomen / das Substantivnoun — a person, animal, thing or idea; always capitalised in German (der Mann, die Katze, das Haus, die Zeit)
  • das Genusgender — maskulin (masculine, der), feminin (feminine, die), neutral (neuter, das). It is grammatical, not logical (das Mädchen = the girl), so learn the article as part of the word.
  • Singular / Pluralsingular (one) / plural (more than one). Plural article is always die.
  • der Kasuscase — the "job" a noun has in the sentence. You know two: Nominativ (nominative) = the subject, asks wer? was?; Akkusativ (accusative) = the direct object, asks wen? was?
  • das Subjektsubject — who or what does the action (Der Vogel isst einen Apfel)
  • das Objektobject — who or what the action is done to (Der Vogel isst einen Apfel)
  • das Verbverb — the action or state word (ist, trinkt, wohnt, möchte); in a statement it is always in position 2
  • das Pronomenpronoun — a word that replaces a noun: ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie, Sie (I, you, he, she, it, we, you all, they, you formal)
  • der Satzsentence
  • das Modalverbmodal verb — a verb like möchten that goes with a second verb in the infinitive at the end
  • der Infinitivinfinitive — the dictionary form of a verb, ending in -en (kaufen, studieren, werden)
  • die W-FrageW-question — a question starting with a W-word (wer, was, wo, wann …)
  • die Endungending — the letters added to a word (mein → meine, meinen)

Befund (what the check of this Heft found)

In September 2026 this whole Heft was checked, lesson by lesson, against the official ÖSD Zertifikat A1 requirements — the Durchführungsbestimmungen (Stand Oktober 2023) and both published Modellsätze. This page records what that check found, what was added because of it, and what to do with the days that are left. Read it once, properly. It changes what you should study.
Die Kurzfassung. (The short version.) Your grammar is not the problem — parts of this Heft are already above A1. Three things were: the exam-training page described the wrong exam; a small set of high-value grammar was genuinely missing (modal verbs above all); and you have never produced anything — no listening, no speaking, no writing under a clock. The grammar holes are about seven hours of work. The production gap is the one that decides whether you pass.

1 · Der ernsteste Befund (the most serious finding)

The old Prüfungstraining page described the Goethe „Start Deutsch 1“ exam, not the ÖSD Zertifikat A1 you are sitting. Six task descriptions were wrong. That is worse than an omission, because it trains you to expect the wrong thing. It has now been rewritten from the official rulebook. These were the errors:

TeilWas hier stand (what it said)Was wirklich kommt (what really comes)
Lesen 1richtig / falsch5 Situationen → 6 Kleinanzeigen, du schreibst eine Zahl · eine Anzeige passt zu nichts
Lesen 2zwei Anzeigen, a oder b3 Anzeigen, je 2 JA/NEIN-Fragen (6 Items)
Lesen 3wieder richtig / falsch5 Texte → 6 Bilder, du schreibst eine Bildnummer
Hören 1Gespräche, zweimal gehört5 Texte → 6 Fotos, NUR EINMAL gehört
Hören 2Durchsagen, einmal gehörtNotizblatt ausfüllen, ZWEIMAL gehört
Hören 3Telefonnachrichten, zweimal5 befragte Personen im Raster, NUR EINMAL
SprechenWortkarten + eine BitteVorstellung · Bildbeschreibung · Rollenspiel zum selben Bild

Two entire Sprechen tasks — the Bildbeschreibung and the Rollenspiel — did not exist anywhere in this Heft. They are 8 of the 25 oral points. The new Sprechkarten section is there for exactly that.

2 · Welche Prüfung du schreibst (which exam you are actually sitting)

There are two ÖSD A1 papers: ÖSD Zertifikat A1 (ZA1) and ÖSD Zertifikat A1 / Österreich (ZA1/Ö). You are sitting ZA1 — not by choice, but by construction. The binding rulebook contains exactly one sentence separating them, and it is geographic:

  • „… ÖSD Zertifikat A1 … an Prüfungszentren weltweit bzw. ÖSD Zertifikat A1 / Österreich an Prüfungszentren in Österreich …“The /Österreich variant can only be administered inside Austria. Durchführungsbestimmungen, Stand Oktober 2023

Pakistan has exactly two licensed ÖSD centres — Karachi and Lahore. There is no mechanism by which a Lahore sitting could hand you the /Ö paper. And it would not matter if it did: TU Chemnitz's condition names issuing organisations, not certificate titles („nur vom Goethe-Institut, Telc-Prüfungszentren oder vom ÖSD“), so either variant satisfies it.

One thing worth un-learning: ZA1 is the broader paper, not the narrower one. Its texts are pluricentric — Berlin and bahn.de in one task, Wien and Graz in another, Swiss francs written CHF 1'200,– in a third. There is no Austrian dialect vocabulary at A1: a scan of both papers for 22 Austriacisms (Jänner, Sackerl, Erdäpfel, Trafik, Matura, Paradeiser …) found zero. Do not spend an hour on it. The one Austrian form worth knowing is Jänner for Januar.

3 · Die Zahlen, die zählen (the numbers that decide it)

ModulTeileZeitPunkteBestanden ab
Schriftliche PrüfungLesen 25 min · Hören ca. 10 min · Schreiben 20 minca. 55 min netto7538
Mündliche PrüfungSprechen, 3 Aufgaben (+10 min Vorbereitungszeit)ca. 10 min2512

Die drei K.-o.-Grenzen (the three knock-outs). Fall below any one of these and the whole written module fails, even with 38+ points in total: Lesen unter 6/30 · Hören unter 6/30 · Schreiben Aufgabe 2 unter 4/10. That last one is the dangerous one, because it is a single 30-word e-mail.

Zwei Punkte pro Fehler — aber nicht pro Item. Each Lesen and Hören Aufgabe is worth 10 points, but the number of items differs, so the conversion table — not a per-item rate — decides. A 5-item Aufgabe runs 5/4/3/2/1/0 richtig → 10/8/6/4/2/0. A 6-item Aufgabe (Lesen Aufgabe 2, the JA/NEIN questions) runs 6/5/4/3/2/1–0 → 10/8/6/4/2/0 — so there the first mistake costs nothing and the second costs two. Either way one careless tick costs far more than 1/5 or 1/6 of the task. And mechanically: genau ein Kreuz pro Zeile (two crosses score zero, exactly like a blank), nie eine Lücke lassen (a wrong guess costs no more than an empty box), and no dictionary is allowed.

An earlier draft of this Heft repeated a claim from a low-quality website that you need 60 %. That is wrong. The official figures are the ones above: 38/75 and 12/25. Also wrong is the „insgesamt 90 Minuten“ printed in the margin of the published Modellsatz — that is stale artwork from 2017. Time your mock exams at 25 / ~10 / 20.

4 · Was gefehlt hat — und jetzt da ist (what was missing, and now is not)

Eleven new Lektionen were written to close the gaps the check found. They are not from your notebook — your tutor never gave you these pages. Each one exists because the exam tests it and this Heft did not have it.

NeuWarum es fehlte und was es kostet
50 ModalverbenThe single densest block of markable grammar on the paper. Most of the six Lesen-Aufgabe-2 JA/NEIN items are modal questions. This Heft taught möchten and wollen — but dürfen existed only inside the waiter's phrase Was darf's denn sein?, and sollen not at all.
51 man + Modalverbman appeared once in 11 000 lines, in Lektion 5, about spelling. Four of the six official Lesen-2 items use it, always with a modal. Parsing Darf man …? instantly is worth more raw marks than anything else on the reading paper.

56 Aushänge & SchilderAnother 10 reading points. The Heft had five sign words. At A1 one keyword decides each match.

60 LieblingsessenA printed topic card in both variants. Lieblings- appeared nowhere, and mögen never appeared as a verb — only möchten.

Plus B · Bildkarten — 61 illustrated vocabulary cards for the objects the picture tasks actually use — and K · Sprechkarten, the speaking training this Heft had no version of.

5 · Was du nicht lernen sollst (what NOT to study — this list saves you days)

This Heft over-taught relative to A1. In September 2026 that surplus was cut out of the lessons, item by item, against the official Goethe A1 word list and both ZA1 Modellsätze — so what is still on the page is A1. The oral criterion for Formale Richtigkeit asks only for „einige wenige einfache grammatische Strukturen und Satzmuster, die sie/er auswendig gelernt hat“ — memorised patterns are enough.

  • Über A1 — gestrichenAbove the level — now cut from this Heft the Partizip-II rule theory (L46) · the haben/sein decision theory (L45) · n-Deklination · the non-A1 verbs in L42 and 100 Verben · Plusquamperfekt (L44) · Ich habe mir das Bein gebrochen (L43). Kept, because A1 needs them: Possessivartikel im Dativ (L35 — in meiner Familie), the er/sie/es forms in 100 Verben, and the Partizip II of common verbs (L46).
  • Klar A2 — gar nicht anfangenClearly A2 — do not start Adjektivendungen vor dem Nomen · Komparativ und Superlativ · weil / dass / ob · TeKaMoLo · deshalb, trotzdem · reflexive Verben als Klasse · die volle Wechselpräpositionen-Tabelle (aber ins Kino & Co. musst du können) · Genitiv

The one exception inside that list: gern → lieber → am liebsten (Lektion 60). That much comparative is A1, because the Lieblings- topic card needs it. Nothing beyond it.

6 · Drei Dinge, die wichtiger sind als jede Grammatik (three things that matter more than any grammar)

  • 📜Beide Module am selben TagSit BOTH modules on 26 September. TU Chemnitz needs a Zertifikat, not a Modulzeugnis. Ungeprüft — bitte schriftlich bestätigen lassen: an earlier version of this page said the Lahore centre reruns ZA1 on 27 and 28 September. A September 2026 re-check could not confirm that, and public listings disagree with this page on both the sitting dates and the venue. ÖSD also recommends waiting about four weeks before a repeat. So plan as if 26 September is your only attempt, and ask the centre in writing whether a same-week retake exists — a retake at the same centre combines into one Gesamtzertifikat, one at a different centre does not.
  • 📅Wann kommt das Zertifikat?26 September → 31 October is about five weeks to mark, issue and physically deliver a paper certificate, and then submit it to the university. That margin — not the exam itself — is the real risk to the admission. Ask the centre this week what date the printed certificate will be in your hands, and tell them the deadline.
  • 📍Der PrüfungsortÖSD's own public exam-date record lists the 26 September sitting at a hotel venue on Egerton Road, not at the centre's usual address. Confirm the address with the centre before the day. Also confirm your oral time slot — the Mündliche Prüfung may be at a different hour.

7 · Der Plan bis zum 26. September (the plan, weighted by marks per hour)

Roughly two hours on new grammar for every ten on production and format. That ratio is the whole plan. Everything below assumes you start today.

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Why the grammar verdict is good news. The check found only five genuinely missing structures — the modals, man, the Wo?-prepositions, es gibt and the five connectors. Everything else the ÖSD A1 inventory asks for was already here, and several things were above it. That is roughly seven hours of new grammar in an eighteen-day run-up. Spend the other hours speaking and listening.
  • Where the marks actually are. Lesen 30 · Hören 30 · Schreiben 15 · Sprechen 25. Hören is tied with Lesen as the biggest single component, and it is the one you have never practised. Treating it as a small slice would be the most expensive mistake available to you.
  • The two once-only tasks. Hören Aufgabe 1 and Aufgabe 3 are played a single time. There is no recovery from a slow start, which is why the daily listening habit matters more than any amount of extra grammar. Before each track: read the questions, decide what kind of thing you are listening for — a price? a platform? a weekday? — and listen for that.
  • On the sources. Everything on this page was checked against ÖSD's own documents rather than against summaries: the Durchführungsbestimmungen (Stand Oktober 2023), the ZA1 and ZA1/Österreich Modellsätze, and TU Chemnitz's own admission wording. Where a source conflicted with another it is flagged above — the 60 % claim and the 90-Minuten margin note are both cases where a secondary source was wrong. If anything here ever contradicts the paper in front of you on the day, the paper wins.
  • One thing this page cannot tell you. Whether your printed certificate will reach you in time for 31 October. That is the only genuinely open risk in the plan, and it is answered by one e-mail to the exam centre, not by studying. Send it this week.
1

Begrüßungen (Greetings)

German greetings run on two dials: the clock, and how close you are to the person. Get those two right and everything else in this Lektion follows.

Die zwei Regeln (the two rules everything hangs on)

1 · Die Uhr — welcher Gruß wann? (the clock — which greeting, when?)

Guten Morgen runs from waking until 11:00, Guten Tag from 11:00 until 18:00, and Guten Abend from 18:00 — while Hallo is safe at any hour with friends. Gute Nacht is not a time slot: it is a farewell, said only when you part late at night or go to bed, never to someone who has just arrived. Real life is fuzzy and nobody checks the clock, but keep to these boundaries while you learn.

🗒️

2 · du oder Sie? (du or Sie?)

du (تم) is for friends, family, classmates and children; Sie (آپ) is for everyone else — strangers, shop staff, officials, teachers, your boss, older people — and polite Sie always keeps its capital S. The choice runs through the whole conversation: Sie travels together with Herr / Frau + surname and with Wie geht es Ihnen? / Und Ihnen?, while du takes the first name and Wie geht es dir? / Und dir? As a learner, use Sie with every adult you do not know until they offer the switch.

🗒️

Die Uhr im Detail (the clock, in detail)
Uhrzeit (time)Gruß (greeting)Hinweis (note)
0–5 Uhr (Nacht / night)Guten Abend!Late night still counts as Abend. Gute Nacht is only for leaving or going to bed.
5–11 Uhr (Morgen / morning)Guten Morgen!From waking until 11:00. In casual speech people shorten it to just "Morgen!"
11–18 Uhr (Tag / day)Guten Tag!11:00 to 18:00 — the safe default with anyone you address as Sie.
18–24 Uhr (Abend / evening)Guten Abend!From 18:00. Still a hello — Gute Nacht is the goodbye.

Begrüßungen (hello-words)
  • 👋Hallo!Hello! /haˈloː/ · hah-LOH · neutral — Any time, almost anyone — leans informal, never wrong with friends.
  • ☀️Guten Tag!Good day! / Hello! /ˌɡuːtn̩ ˈtaːk/ · goo-tn TAHK · formell — 11:00 until 18:00 — shops, offices, strangers; the safe all-day default.
  • 🌅Guten Morgen!Good morning! /ˌɡuːtn̩ ˈmɔʁɡn̩/ · goo-tn MO-uh-gn · formell — From waking until 11:00 — with strangers, shop staff and at work.
  • 🌆Guten Abend!Good evening! /ˌɡuːtn̩ ˈaːbn̩t/ · goo-tn AH-bnt · formell — From 18:00 — arriving at a dinner, a restaurant, a host's door.
  • ⛰️Grüß Gott!Hello! (literally "God greet you") /ˌɡʁyːs ˈɡɔt/ · grewss GOT · regional — Bavaria, Austria, Swabia — to anyone, any hour; the Guten Tag of the south.
  • 🤗Grüß dich!Hi! /ˈɡʁyːs dɪç/ · GREWSS dikh · regional — South only, and only to someone you say du to — a friend or a child.
  • 🙏Grüß Sie!Hello! /ˈɡʁyːs ziː/ · GREWSS zee · regional — South, to a Sie-person; polite but colloquial — Guten Tag is safer with officials.
  • 👥Hallo zusammen!Hello everyone! /haˌloː tsuˈzamən/ · hah-loh tsoo-ZAM-n · neutral — Walking into a room — greet everyone at once instead of one by one.
Verabschiedungen (goodbye-words)
  • 🌙Gute Nacht!Good night! /ˌɡuːtə ˈnaxt/ · goo-tuh NAKHT · neutral — Only when parting late at night or before sleep — never a hello.
  • 👋Tschüs! / Tschüss!Bye! /tʃyːs/ · /tʃʏs/ · CHEWSS · CHYUSS · informell — Leaving friends, colleagues, shop staff; both spellings standard, never in a letter.
  • 🚶Auf Wiedersehen!Goodbye (see you again) /aʊ̯f ˈviːdɐˌzeːən/ · owf VEE-duh-zay-n · formell — Leaving face to face — safe with strangers, older people, formal settings.
  • ☎️Auf Wiederhören!Goodbye (on the phone) /aʊ̯f ˈviːdɐˌhøːʁən/ · owf VEE-duh-h-oe-rn · formell — Ending a phone call — hören = to hear, and you only hear each other.
  • ⏳Bis bald!See you soon! /bɪs ˈbalt/ · bis BALT · neutral — Leaving when you will meet again soon, with no fixed date.
  • 🕒Bis später!See you later! /bɪs ˈʃpɛːtɐ/ · bis SHPAY-tuh · neutral — Leaving when you really will meet again the same day.
  • 🌞Schönen Tag noch!Have a nice rest of the day! /ˌʃøːnən ˈtaːk nɔx/ · sh-oe-nn TAHK nokh · neutral — Leaving a shop, a bakery or an office — heard more often than Auf Wiedersehen.
  • 🙌Danke, gleichfalls!Thanks, same to you! /ˈdaŋkə, ˈɡlaɪ̯çfals/ · DANG-kuh, GL-EYE-kh-fals · neutral — Two-word reply to any good wish someone gives you as you part.
  • 📅Bis morgen!See you tomorrow! /bɪs ˈmɔʁɡn̩/ · bis MO-uh-gn · neutral — Leaving when you will see the person again tomorrow (small m = tomorrow).
Beides (works both ways — hello and goodbye)
  • 🤝Servus!Hi! / Bye! /ˈzɛʁvʊs/ · ZEH-uh-vus · regional — Austria, Bavaria and southern Germany; du only — works arriving and leaving.
  • 🍽️Mahlzeit!literally "mealtime" /ˈmaːltsaɪ̯t/ · MAHL-ts-EYE-t · informell — Workplace only — canteens, corridors, offices, ~11:30–14:00. Never to shop staff or strangers.
Gesprochen oder geschrieben? (spoken or written?)
  • 🗣️Guten Tag, Herr Weber!Hello, Mr Weber! — a safe formal greeting face to face.
  • ✉️Sehr geehrter Herr Weber,Dear Mr Weber, — the standard formal written salutation to a man.

Dialog 1 — Im Büro(at the office)

9 Uhr, erster Arbeitstag (9 a.m., first day at work)
🧑 Herr Weber
Guten Morgen!Good morning!
👩 Frau Klein
Guten Morgen! Ich heiße Anna Klein. Und Sie?Good morning! My name is Anna Klein. And you?
🧑 Herr Weber
Ich bin Thomas Weber. Freut mich!I am Thomas Weber. Pleased to meet you!
👩 Frau Klein
Freut mich auch, Herr Weber!Pleased to meet you too, Mr Weber!
🧑 Herr Weber
Wie geht es Ihnen, Frau Klein?How are you, Ms Klein?
👩 Frau Klein
Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?Fine, thanks. And you?
🧑 Herr Weber
Danke, auch gut. Bis später!Fine too, thanks. See you later!
17 Uhr (5 p.m.)
👩 Frau Klein
Auf Wiedersehen, Herr Weber!Goodbye, Mr Weber!
🧑 Herr Weber
Auf Wiedersehen, Frau Klein!Goodbye, Ms Klein!

A natural order for this first meeting is greeting → names → Freut mich! → only then Wie geht es Ihnen? Answer Freut mich! with Freut mich auch!; in very formal settings you may also hear Sehr angenehm!

Dialog 2 — Auf der Straße(in the street, 15 Uhr / 3 p.m.)

Max rempelt jemanden an (Max bumps into someone)
🧑 Max
Entschuldigung!Sorry!
👩 Lisa
Hallo, Max!Hi, Max!
🧑 Max
Grüß dich, Lisa! Wie geht's?Hi, Lisa! How are you?
👩 Lisa
Danke, gut. Und dir?Fine, thanks. And you?
🧑 Max
Auch gut, danke.Good too, thanks.
👩 Lisa
Tschüs! Bis später!Bye! See you later!
🧑 Max
Tschüs, Lisa!Bye, Lisa!

Grüß dich carries dich inside it (the du side), so keep it for friends; it is heard mostly in southern Germany, while Hallo works everywhere. With someone you address as Sie, say Guten Tag (in the south you may also hear Grüß Sie). Tschüs and Tschüss are both standard spellings; Tschüss is the more frequent one today.

Dialog 3 — Am Telefon(on the telephone, 14 Uhr / 2 p.m.)

☎️ Herr Schmidt
Schmidt.Schmidt speaking. / (فون اٹھاتے ہوئے) شمٹ بول رہا ہوں
👩 Frau Braun
Guten Tag, Herr Schmidt! Hier ist Julia Braun.Hello, Mr Schmidt! This is Julia Braun.
☎️ Herr Schmidt
Ja, guten Tag, Frau Braun! Wie geht es Ihnen?Yes, hello, Ms Braun! How are you?
👩 Frau Braun
Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?Fine, thanks. And you?
☎️ Herr Schmidt
Danke, auch gut.Fine too, thanks.
👩 Frau Braun
Auf Wiederhören, Herr Schmidt!Goodbye, Mr Schmidt! (on the phone)
☎️ Herr Schmidt
Auf Wiederhören! Bis bald!Goodbye! See you soon!

In Germany people usually answer the phone with their family name (Schmidt.), and you introduce yourself with Hier ist …, not Ich bin …. On the phone you do not see the other person, you hear them — so hören, not sehen: Auf Wieder·hören is the expected phone goodbye. Plenty of people still say Auf Wiedersehen on the phone; that is common and not an error. Among friends, Tschüs on the phone is normal.

Dialog 4 — In der Bäckerei in Bayern(at the bakery in Bavaria)

🧑 Stefan
Grüß Gott!Hello! (southern)
👩 Frau Huber
Grüß Gott! Herr Bauer?Hello! Mr Bauer?
🧑 Stefan
Nein, ich heiße Stefan Wagner.No, my name is Stefan Wagner.
👩 Frau Huber
Entschuldigung, Herr Wagner! Wie geht es Ihnen?Sorry, Mr Wagner! How are you?
🧑 Stefan
Danke, gut!Fine, thanks!
👩 Frau Huber
Auf Wiedersehen, Herr Wagner!Goodbye, Mr Wagner!
🧑 Stefan
Auf Wiedersehen!Goodbye!
vor der Bäckerei (outside the bakery, Stefan meets his friend Toni)
🧑 Toni
Servus, Stefan!Hi, Stefan!
🧑 Stefan
Servus, Toni! Bis bald!Bye, Toni! See you soon!

In Bavaria and Austria Grüß Gott is the everyday Guten Tag — the baker uses it with a customer she does not know, and it stays polite. Servus (Austria, Bavaria, southern Germany) works in both directions — hello and goodbye — but it is informal (du), so it belongs with friends like Toni, not with a customer.

Dialog 5 — Abendessen bei Familie Roth(dinner at the Roths')

19 Uhr, an der Tür (7 p.m., at the door)
👩 Frau Roth
Guten Abend, Herr Neumann!Good evening, Mr Neumann!
🧑 Herr Neumann
Guten Abend, Frau Roth! Wie geht es Ihnen?Good evening, Ms Roth! How are you?
👩 Frau Roth
Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?Fine, thanks. And you?
🧑 Herr Neumann
Danke, auch gut.Fine too, thanks.
später, 23 Uhr (later, 11 p.m.)
🧑 Herr Neumann
Auf Wiedersehen, Frau Roth! Gute Nacht!Goodbye, Ms Roth! Good night!
👩 Frau Roth
Gute Nacht! Bis bald!Good night! See you soon!

Guten Abend greets people from 18:00. Gute Nacht is not a time slot at all — it is a parting line for late at night or before sleep, never a hello. And watch the ending: Gute Nacht (die Nacht) but Guten Morgen / Tag / Abend (der Morgen, der Tag, der Abend).

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Wie geht es Ihnen? (asking how someone is, formal)
WieW-Wort · question wordgehtVerb · position 2esSubjekt · "it"Ihnen?formal "to you" · Dativ

The idiom is literally "how goes it to you?" — es is the grammatical subject, and Ihnen (capital I) is the formal "you". The verb geht still sits in position 2, right after the W-word Wie. To a friend, swap in the du-form: Wie geht es dir?

2 · Ich heiße + Name (giving your name)
IchSubjekt · subjectheißeVerb · position 2Anna Klein.Name, not Akkusativ

heißen (to be called) works like sein — the name that follows is not an object, so it stays in the plain form, never einen or -en. Asking: Wie heißen Sie? (formal) / Wie heißt du? (informal).

3 · Ich bin + Name (the other way to introduce yourself)
IchSubjekt · subjectbinVerb · position 2Thomas Weber.Name

Ich bin … and Ich heiße … both introduce your name and are used side by side in Dialog 1 — Herr Weber opens with Ich bin, Frau Klein with Ich heiße. Either is correct; heißen is slightly more common for names alone.

4 · Wie geht's? / Und dir? (the informal ping-pong)
WieW-Wortgeht's?= geht es · VerbUnd dir?informal "and you"

geht's is the spoken contraction of geht es. Answering Gut, danke and stopping there sounds cold — always send the question back: Und dir? to a friend, Und Ihnen? formally.

5 · Herr / Frau + Nachname (never the first name with Sie)
HerrtitleWeber,Nachname · surnamewieW-WortgehtVerbesSubjektIhnen?capital Sie-forms

Herr and Frau pair with the family name when used with a person's name — Herr Weber, never Herr Thomas. Whenever Sie / Ihnen / Ihr appears, the capital letter is part of the grammar, not a typo.

6 · Hier ist … (introducing yourself on the phone)
HierOrt · "here", position 1istVerb · position 2Julia Braun.Subjekt, after the verb

Start the sentence with something other than the subject — here Hier — and the verb still claims position 2, pushing the subject to third place. On the phone, Hier ist Julia Braun is the conventional way to identify yourself; Ich bin Julia Braun is grammatically correct but is not the usual telephone formula.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Auf Wiedersehen / Auf Wiederhören (face-to-face / phone goodbye): Wiedersehen holds sehen = to see → say it face to face. Wiederhören holds hören = to hear → say it on the phone.
  • Gute Nacht (Good night) has no -n: at night the N goes to sleep — Gute Nacht. By day the N is awake — Guten Tag, Guten Morgen, Guten Abend.
  • Grüß Gott (southern hello) lives in the mountains: the closer to the Alps, the more God is in the greeting. Flat, rainy Hamburg keeps it plain: Guten Tag or the northern Moin.
  • Servus (hello / goodbye): from Latin servus = servant, "at your service" — a servant bows both when you arrive and when you leave, so one word covers hello and goodbye.
  • The ü in Tschüs: say Urdu ای and hold it, then — without moving the tongue — squeeze the lips into a whistle circle: Tschüs = "CHEWSS". Careful: später has ä instead — lips stay flat.
  • Das deutsche R (the German R): the German r gargles in the throat — think غ (as in غزل), not the Urdu ر. In Grüß Gott it comes from the throat, like clearing it politely.
  • Wie geht's? (How are you?) is ping-pong, not a wall: Gut, danke is only half the move — hit the ball back with Und dir? or Und Ihnen?
  • bald ≠ گنجا: German bald means "soon" — the hair grows back soon! Bis bald = see you soon, no fixed time; Bis später = later the same day.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Guten Nacht! → Gute Nacht! (goo-tuh NAKHT) — Nacht is a die-word, so Gute; Tag, Morgen and Abend are der-words, so Guten.
  • Gute Tag! → Guten Tag! (goo-tn TAHK) — same rule the other way round: Guten Tag, Guten Morgen, Guten Abend — always -n.
  • Tschuss! → Tschüs! (CHEWSS) or Tschüss! (CHYUSS) — both spellings are standard, but the ü is not optional — never a plain u.
  • (on the phone) Auf Wiedersehen! → Auf Wiederhören! (owf VEE-duh-hur-rn) — sehen = see, hören = hear, and on the phone you only hear each other.
  • Herr Thomas, wie geht es Ihnen? (to Thomas Weber) → Herr Weber, wie geht es Ihnen? — Herr (جناب) and Frau (محترمہ) go with the family name, not the first name.
  • — Wie geht's? — Gut. (and nothing else) → Gut, danke. Und dir? / Und Ihnen? — the question is a two-way ball: answer, then send it back, or you sound cold.
  • (to a stranger) Grüß dich! → Grüß Gott! (grewss GOT) / Guten Tag! — dich is the du-form; a Sie-person gets Grüß Gott in the south, Guten Tag elsewhere.
  • (to your professor, when unsure) Tschüs! → Auf Wiedersehen! (owf VEE-duh-zay-n) — Tschüs is informal; Auf Wiedersehen is never wrong while you are still listening in.
  • (arriving at 20:00) Gute Nacht! → Guten Abend! — Gute Nacht is not a time slot — only for parting late at night or going to bed.
  • (in Hamburg) Grüß Gott! → Guten Tag! / Moin! (MOYN, informal) — Grüß Gott is southern — Bayern, Baden-Württemberg, Österreich; in the north it sounds out of place.
2

Häufige Redemittel (common phrases)

The phrases that keep a conversation alive when your German runs out. Wie bitte? and Noch einmal, bitte! buy you a second try at every sentence you miss.

Die zwei Regeln (the two rules that carry this Lektion)

1 · bitte — ein Wort, drei Aufgaben (bitte — one word, three jobs)

bitte means please, you're welcome and here you are — and as a question, Wie bitte? means pardon? It all comes from the verb bitten, "to ask". One warning: answering an offer with a bare Danke is usually heard as no thanks. If you want the thing, say Ja, bitte!

2 · kein oder nicht? (kein or nicht?)

kein negates an indefinite or articleless noun phrase: kein Deutsch, kein Problem, keine Ahnung. nicht negates a verb, adjective or whole statement: Ich verstehe nicht, Ich weiß nicht. For these examples, the test is: if you could say a / an / any in the English sentence, use kein. And die-words pull an -e onto it — die Ahnung → keine Ahnung, exactly like Gute Nacht in Lektion 1.

Wortschatz 1 (vocabulary 1) · Danken, Bitten, Entschuldigen

Danken (thanking)
  • 🙏Danke!Thanks! DANG-kuh · — the everyday thank-you; alone, in answer to an offer, it reads as "no thanks".
  • 🙏Danke schön!Thank you kindly! DANG-kuh SH-OE-n · — a warmer Danke; schön stays lowercase, it is an adjective, not a noun.
  • 🙏Vielen Dank!Thank you very much! FEE-ln DANK · — the strongest of the three; v is said f.
Bitten (asking / offering)
  • 🤲Bitte!You're welcome! / Please! BIT-uh · — three jobs: please, you're welcome, here you are; context decides.
  • 🍽️Bitte schön!You're welcome! / Here you are! BIT-uh SH-OE-n · — what the waiter says as the plate lands.
  • ✅Ja, bitte!Yes, please! yah, BIT-uh · — say this to accept an offer; a bare Danke would be heard as no.
Entschuldigen (apologising)
  • 🙇Entschuldigen Sie, bitte!Excuse me, please! ent-SHUL-di-gn zee, BIT-uh · — verb + Sie: the polite opener before you ask a stranger anything · formell
  • 😳Entschuldigung!Excuse me! / Sorry! ent-SHUL-di-gung · — a noun used as a neutral apology or polite attention-getter, so it works with anyone; in informal situations it often replaces a full verb phrase.
  • 💔Es tut mir leid!I am sorry! es toot mee-uh L-EYE-t · — real regret, not small bumps; learn as one block, word-for-word it is nonsense.

Wortschatz 2 (vocabulary 2) · Nachfragen, Sprachen

Nachfragen (asking again)
  • ❓Wie bitte?Pardon? / Sorry, what? vee BIT-uh · — you did not HEAR it; never say Was? to a stranger.
  • 🔁Noch einmal, bitte!Once again, please! nokh EYE-n-mahl, BIT-uh · — asks for a repeat; noch = more, einmal = one time.
  • 🔁Bitte wiederholen Sie!Please repeat! BIT-uh vee-duh-HOH-ln zee · — a Sie-command: verb first, Sie second, bitte to soften · formell
  • 😕Ich verstehe nicht.I don't understand. ikh feh-uh-SHTAY-uh nikht · — you HEARD it, the meaning is what escaped; nicht goes last.
Sprachen (languages)
  • 🇩🇪Sprechen Sie Deutsch?Do you speak German? SHPREKH-n zee DOYTCH · — sp- at the start is said shp-; eu = oy · formell
  • 🇬🇧Sprechen Sie Englisch?Do you speak English? SHPREKH-n zee ENG-lish · — language names are nouns, so they take a capital letter · formell
  • 🚫Ich spreche kein Deutsch.I don't speak German. ikh SHPREKH-uh k-EYE-n DOYTCH · — kein because Deutsch is a noun, never nicht Deutsch.
  • 🤏Ich spreche etwas Deutsch.I speak a bit of German. ikh SHPREKH-uh ET-vas DOYTCH · — better than kein, it makes people slow down instead of switching to English.

Wortschatz 3 (vocabulary 3) · Antworten, Regeln

Antworten (answering)
  • 🤷Ich weiß nicht.I don't know. ikh V-EYE-ss nikht · — safe anywhere, including with your boss.
  • 💭Keine Ahnung!No idea! K-EYE-nuh AH-nung · — casual, friends only; die Ahnung is a die-word, so kein takes -e · informell
  • 👍Kein Problem!No problem! k-EYE-n pro-BLAYM · — the standard answer when someone apologises to you.
  • ⏳Einen Moment, bitte!One moment, please! EYE-nn mo-MENT, BIT-uh · — buys you a few seconds without sounding rude.
  • ✅Ja.Yes. yah · — the j is said like an English y.
  • ❌Nein.No. N-EYE-n · — ei = EYE; do not confuse with kein, which negates a noun.
  • 🤔Vielleicht.Maybe. fee-L-EYE-kht · — v = f, ei = EYE, ch = the soft kh.
Regel (the rules, in short)
  • 📐kein oder nicht?kein negates an indefinite or articleless noun phrase · nicht negates a verb, adjective or statement — in these examples, if you could say a/an/any in English, use kein: kein Deutsch, keine Ahnung, kein Problem.
  • 📐Warum keine Ahnung?die Ahnung is a die-word, so kein takes -e — same pattern as Gute Nacht in Lektion 1: die-words pull an -e onto the word in front.
  • 🔢Verb auf Platz 2in a main-clause statement, the conjugated verb is the second block — Ich (1) spreche (2) … · Jetzt (1) verstehe (2) ich; Urdu puts the verb last, while a German statement puts it second.
  • ⚖️Entschuldigung oder Es tut mir leid?small bump vs. real regret — Entschuldigung to squeeze past; Es tut mir leid when you are actually sorry.
Nomen (nouns: article and plural)
  • 🙏der Dank · Plural: —thanks, gratitude · no usual plural
  • 😳die Entschuldigung · die Entschuldigungenapology / excuse · apologies / excuses
  • 💭die Ahnung · die Ahnungenidea / inkling · ideas / inklings
  • ⚠️das Problem · die Problemeproblem · problems
  • ⏱️der Moment · die Momentemoment · moments
  • 🇩🇪das Deutsch · Plural: —the German language · no plural
  • 🇬🇧das Englisch · Plural: —the English language · no plural

Dialoge (dialogues)

Dialog 1 · Im Zug (on the train)
Sara needs to get past a stranger
👩 Sara
Entschuldigung!Excuse me!
🧔 Mann
Ja, bitte?Yes?
👩 Sara
Danke schön!Thank you kindly!
🧔 Mann
Bitte!You're welcome!

Four lines, and bitte appears twice with two different meanings — first "how can I help?", then "you're welcome". Context does all the work.

Dialog 2 · Zu schnell (too fast)
👩 Frau Klein
Guten Tag! Sprechen Sie Deutsch?Hello! Do you speak German?
🧑 Ali
Ich spreche etwas Deutsch.I speak a bit of German.
Frau Klein speaks quickly
🧑 Ali
Wie bitte? Noch einmal, bitte!Pardon? Once again, please!
she repeats, slowly
🧑 Ali
Danke! Jetzt verstehe ich.Thanks! Now I understand.

etwas Deutsch beats kein Deutsch — it makes people slow down instead of switching to English. In the last line Jetzt takes slot 1, so the verb verstehe takes slot 2 and ich moves behind it. In a main-clause statement, the conjugated verb stays in position two.

Dialog 3 · Kein Englisch (no English)
🧳 Tourist
Entschuldigen Sie, bitte! Sprechen Sie Englisch?Excuse me, please! Do you speak English?
👨 Herr Weber
Nein, ich spreche kein Englisch. Es tut mir leid!No, I don't speak English. I'm sorry!
🧳 Tourist
Kein Problem. Danke!No problem. Thanks!
👨 Herr Weber
Bitte. Auf Wiedersehen!You're welcome. Goodbye!
🧳 Tourist
Auf Wiedersehen!Goodbye!

kein Englisch (a noun) but Es tut mir leid as a fixed block. They part with Auf Wiedersehen, not Tschüs, because these two are strangers on Sie terms.

Dialog 4 · Am Schalter (at the counter)
👩 Frau Ott
Guten Morgen! Einen Moment, bitte!Good morning! One moment, please!
🧑 Bilal
Ja, natürlich.Yes, of course.
👩 Frau Ott
Wie ist Ihr Familienname?What is your surname?
🧑 Bilal
Wie bitte? Bitte wiederholen Sie!Pardon? Please repeat!
👩 Frau Ott
Ihr Familienname, bitte!Your surname, please!
🧑 Bilal
Ah! Ahmad.Ah! Ahmad.
👩 Frau Ott
Danke schön!Thank you kindly!

Wiederholen Sie! is the Sie-command — verb first, Sie second, bitte to soften. The question Wie ist Ihr Familienname? belongs to Lektion 7; it is here only so the scene works.

Dialog 5 · Keine Ahnung (no idea — two friends, du)
👩 Lena
Hallo! Wie spät ist es?Hi! What time is it?
🧑 Max
Keine Ahnung! Ich weiß nicht.No idea! I don't know.
👩 Lena
Kein Problem. Tschüs!No problem. Bye!
🧑 Max
Tschüs! Bis später!Bye! See you later!

Keine Ahnung is casual, so it fits between friends; to a stranger use Ich weiß nicht. Both negations sit side by side here: Keine Ahnung (noun → kein) and Ich weiß nicht (verb → nicht).

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · kein negates an indefinite noun phrase — object slot
IchSubjekt · subjectsprecheVerb · position 2kein DeutschObjekt · negated noun phrase

Ich spreche kein Deutsch. (I don't speak German.) The articleless noun phrase Deutsch is negated with kein here, not nicht — compare the accusative pattern in Lektion 27.

2 · nicht negates the statement — last in this short sentence
IchSubjekt · subjectversteheVerb · position 2nichtRest · negation, end position here

Ich verstehe nicht. (I don't understand.) Here nicht negates the statement and comes last because nothing else follows; its position can change in longer sentences.

3 · Wie bitte? — a question with no verb
WieW-Wort · question wordbitte?fixed pair · no verb needed

Wie bitte? (Pardon?) is a frozen chunk — wie (how) plus bitte stand in for a whole sentence like "how, please, did you say that again?" Do not try to build a full sentence around it.

4 · Sie-Befehl (formal command): Verb + Sie + …!
BittepleasewiederholenVerb · position 1Sie!Subjekt · right after verb

Bitte wiederholen Sie! (Please repeat!) The formal command puts the verb first and Sie straight after it — the same Sie-Imperativ pattern as Kommen Sie mit! in Lektion 30. bitte only softens; it never moves the verb.

5 · Ja/Nein-Frage (yes/no question): Verb + Sie + Objekt?
SprechenVerb · position 1SieSubjekt · subjectDeutsch?Objekt · language name

Sprechen Sie Deutsch? (Do you speak German?) A yes/no question sends the verb to position 1; Sie follows immediately. Language names are capitalised nouns, so they sit in the object slot like Block 1.

6 · Verb auf Platz 2 (verb in position 2) — statements
JetztZeit · time, position 1versteheVerb · position 2ichSubjekt · moves after the verb

Jetzt verstehe ich. (Now I understand.) Put ich first instead and the verb still lands in slot 2 — Ich verstehe jetzt. works too. In a main-clause statement, the conjugated verb occupies position 2; yes/no questions and commands, as Blocks 4–5 show, place it first.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • bitte = "I ask": bitten = to ask. Please, you're welcome, here you are — all three are "I ask you". One word, one idea.
  • Danke → Bitte: a closed loop, like. One comes at you, the other goes back — no thinking required.
  • kein kills a Noun: as a starter mnemonic, kein often points to a capitalised noun. More precisely, it negates an indefinite or articleless noun phrase: kein Problem, kein Deutsch.
  • keine Ahnung, die Ahnung: both end in -e. The die-word drags its -e onto kein.
  • Ahnung ≈ "an inkling": Keine Ahnung = not even an inkling.
  • Deutsch = DOYTCH: eu is the oy in boy. Say "boy", then "Doytch". Never "dutch" — that is a different country.
  • v is f: Vielen Dank starts like Film. German v borrowed English's f and never gave it back.
  • sp = shp: German shushes before it speaks: sprechen → shprechen.
  • Verb auf Platz 2: in a statement, count blocks, not words: Ich (1) spreche (2). Put another block in slot 1 and the conjugated verb still lands on 2.
  • Ohren oder Kopf? (ears or head?): did not reach your ears → Wie bitte? Reached your ears but not your head → Ich verstehe nicht. See the figure above.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Ich spreche nicht Deutsch. → Ich spreche kein Deutsch. — Deutsch is a noun → kein.
  • Kein Ahnung! → Keine Ahnung! — die Ahnung is a die-word → -e.
  • Ich nicht verstehe. → Ich verstehe nicht. — in this statement, the verb is second; nicht comes last.
  • Ich tue nicht wissen. → Ich weiß nicht. — German has no do / don't helper verb.
  • (offered tea, you want it) Danke! → Ja, bitte! — a bare Danke is heard as a refusal.
  • (to a stranger) Was? → Wie bitte? — Was? is blunt to the point of rude.
  • (you bumped someone) Es tut mir leid! → Entschuldigung! — for a small bump, Entschuldigung is the usual choice; Es tut mir leid normally expresses deeper regret.
  • (to your boss) Keine Ahnung! → Ich weiß nicht. — Keine Ahnung is casual.
  • Sprechen sie Deutsch? → Sprechen Sie Deutsch? — polite Sie always takes a capital S.
  • Danke Schön! → Danke schön! — schön is an adjective, no capital letter.
3

Zahlen 0–20 (Numbers 0–20)

Twenty-one words, four of which catch every beginner. Learn those four properly and German counting all the way to a million falls out of them.

Die zwei Regeln (the two rules that carry this Lektion)

z = ts, s = z
German z is always the ts of English cats — zwei is TSV-EYE, zehn is TSAYN. The buzzing English z sound does exist, but it is written s: sieben = ZEE-bn, sechs = ZEKS. The two letters have swapped jobs, and fixing this one habit repairs half your counting.
Drei Schichten, nicht einundzwanzig Wörter (three layers, not twenty-one words)
Only 0–12 must be memorised. 13–19 is a pattern — number + zehn, exactly English's -teen. Two words shorten inside that pattern because the full form is unsayable: sechs loses its s (sechzehn) and sieben loses its en (siebzehn). Those same two shorten again in Lektion 4, so you learn the reason once and get both lessons.

Zahlen 0–20 (the full number line)

A number appears — say it in German out loud, then uncover it. Use the arrow to flip the direction.

0 null 1 eins 2 zwei 3 drei 4 vier 5 fünf 6 sechs 7 sieben 8 acht 9 neun 10 zehn 11 elf 12 zwölf 13 dreizehn 14 vierzehn 15 fünfzehn 16 sechzehn 17 siebzehn 18 achtzehn 19 neunzehn 20 zwanzig

Zahl (number — the counting words)

  • 0️⃣nullzero — in phone numbers Germans say null for 0; unlike English, standard German does not substitute "oh". NUL ·
  • 1️⃣einsone (counting) — use eins to count or when the number stands alone; before a noun it becomes ein-. EYE-ns ·
  • 2️⃣zweitwo — z = ts. On the phone Germans often say zwo instead, so it cannot be heard as drei. TSV-EYE ·

Stolperfalle (trap — the eight everyone gets wrong)

  • 1️⃣1️⃣elfeleven — German broke the -zehn pattern at 11 and 12, exactly where English broke it too. ELF ·
  • 1️⃣2️⃣zwölftwelve — the ö is compulsory. z = ts, so it starts TSV-, never ZV-. TSV-OE-LF ·
  • 5️⃣fünffive — round your lips as if to whistle, then say "eenf". No pucker, no fünf. FEWNF ·
  • 6️⃣sechssix — chs = ks, so it sounds like English "zeks". The s buzzes; it is not an English s. ZEKS ·
  • 1️⃣4️⃣vierzehnfourteen — vier alone has a long ee (FEE-uh), but vierzehn shortens it. Same in vierzig, Lektion 4. FEER-tsayn ·
  • 1️⃣6️⃣sechzehnsixteen — sechs drops its s: sechs-zehn would crash four consonants together. Never sechszehn. ZEKH-tsayn ·
  • 1️⃣7️⃣siebzehnseventeen — sieben drops its en. Never siebenzehn. Both words diet again in Lektion 4. ZEEP-tsayn ·
  • 2️⃣0️⃣zwanzigtwenty — in standard German, final -ig is said -ikh, never like English pig. This also applies to the numbers ending in -zig in Lektion 4. TSVAN-tsikh ·

Am Telefon (on the phone)

  • 📞zwotwo (on the phone) — zwei and drei rhyme, so a bad line confuses them; zwo removes the ambiguity. Recognise it. TSVOH ·
  • 📱Wie ist Ihre Handynummer?What is your mobile number? (Sie) — Handy is a German word for a mobile; no English speaker uses it that way. vee ist EE-ruh HEN-dee-num-uh ·
  • 📱Wie ist deine Handynummer?What is your mobile number? (du) — Ihre → deine; the grammar behind it comes in Lektion 7. vee ist D-EYE-nuh HEN-dee-num-uh ·
  • 📇Meine Handynummer ist …My mobile number is … — then read the digits one at a time, never as whole numbers. M-EYE-nuh HEN-dee-num-uh ist ·
  • 🐢Langsam, bitte!Slowly, please! — pairs with Noch einmal, bitte! from Lektion 2 when a number goes past too fast. LANG-zahm, BIT-uh ·

Regel (rule — four one-line reminders)

  • 🐈z = tsGerman z is always ts, never English z — and s before a vowel buzzes like English z. The two letters swapped jobs: sieben = ZEE-bn.
  • 🔟-zehn = -teen13–19 are just number + zehn — dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn … seven of the twenty-one words come free.
  • ❓eins oder ein?eins counts or stands alone; an inflected form of ein- goes before a noun — eins, zwei, drei … but Einen Moment, bitte! — never Eins Moment.
  • 🔢Nummer oder Zahl?Nummer labels, Zahl counts — your phone, house and room have a Nummer; a quantity is a Zahl.

Nomen aus dieser Lektion (nouns used in this lesson)

  • 📱die Handynummer / die Handynummernmobile (phone) number
  • 🔢die Nummer / die Nummernnumber that identifies something — phone, house, room
  • ➕die Zahl / die Zahlennumber that measures a quantity
  • ⏳der Moment / die Momentemoment · Einen Moment, bitte! (just a moment, please!)
  • ❗das Problem / die Problemeproblem · Kein Problem! (no problem!)
  • 🔟die Ziffer / die Zifferndigit — a single number 0–9 read on its own

Dialog 1 (Die Handynummer · the mobile number)

👩 Frau Ott
Guten Tag! Wie ist Ihre Handynummer?Hello! What is your mobile number?
🧑 Bilal
Meine Handynummer ist null – eins – sieben – sechs – vier – fünf – zwei – drei – acht – neun – eins.My mobile number is 0-1-7-6-4-5-2-3-8-9-1.
👩 Frau Ott
Noch einmal, bitte! Langsam!Once again, please! Slowly!
🧑 Bilal
Null – eins – sieben – sechs … vier – fünf – zwo – drei … acht – neun – eins.0-1-7-6 … 4-5-2-3 … 8-9-1.
👩 Frau Ott
Danke schön!Thank you kindly!
🧑 Bilal
Bitte!You're welcome!

The second time round Bilal says zwo instead of zwei, exactly as a German would, so it cannot be confused with drei. Note also that the digits come in groups with a pause — never as whole numbers.

Dialog 2 (Wie viele? · how many? — two friends, du)

👩 Lena
Hallo! Wie viele?Hi! How many?
👨 Max
Sechzehn.Sixteen.
👩 Lena
Wie bitte? Sechs oder sechzehn?Pardon? Six or sixteen?
👨 Max
Sechzehn! Eins – sechs.Sixteen! One – six.
👩 Lena
Ah, danke!Ah, thanks!

When a number is misheard, Germans read out the digits: Eins – sechs removes all doubt. oder = or and wie viele = how many are bonus words — recognise only.

Dialog 3 (Im Hotel · at the hotel)

🙋 Gast
Guten Abend!Good evening!
🛎️ Rezeption
Guten Abend! Zimmer zwölf.Good evening! Room twelve.
🙋 Gast
Wie bitte? Zwei?Pardon? Two?
🛎️ Rezeption
Nein — zwölf. Eins – zwei.No — twelve. One – two.
🙋 Gast
Ah, zwölf. Vielen Dank!Ah, twelve. Thank you very much!
🛎️ Rezeption
Bitte schön. Gute Nacht!You're welcome. Good night!
🙋 Gast
Gute Nacht!Good night!

Gute Nacht is right here because the guest is leaving for the night — it is a farewell, never a hello (Lektion 1). Zimmer = room is recognise-only.

Dialog 4 (Falsch verbunden · wrong number)

🗣️ Stimme
Schmidt.Schmidt (speaking).
☎️ Anrufer
Guten Tag! Ist das null – drei – drei – acht?Hello! Is that 0-3-3-8?
🗣️ Stimme
Nein. Hier ist null – drei – drei – neun.No. This is 0-3-3-9.
☎️ Anrufer
Oh! Entschuldigung! Es tut mir leid!Oh! Excuse me! I'm sorry!
🗣️ Stimme
Kein Problem. Auf Wiederhören!No problem. Goodbye!
☎️ Anrufer
Auf Wiederhören!Goodbye!

Three earlier habits in one short call: answering with the surname only, Auf Wiederhören because it is a phone, and Es tut mir leid because this is a real inconvenience rather than a small bump.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Wie + ist + Subjekt? — asking for a number
WieW-Wort · question wordistVerb · position 2Ihre Handynummer?Subjekt · subject

Wie ist Ihre Handynummer? (formal) / Wie ist deine Handynummer? (informal — Lektion 7 has the grammar behind Ihre → deine). The verb still sits in position 2, straight after the W-word, exactly like every other W-question.

2 · Meine Handynummer ist … + Rest — reading the digits
Meine HandynummerSubjekt · subjectistVerb · position 2null – eins – sieben – sechs …Rest · one digit at a time

Once ist has done its job, this clarity-first pattern gives the digits one at a time rather than reading the phone number as one huge Zahl. Compare the Korrekturen below for that classic beginner mistake.

3 · Yes/no question: verb first
IstVerb · position 1dasSubjekt · subjectnull – drei – drei – acht?Rest · digits

From Dialog 4: Ist das null – drei – drei – acht? A yes/no question always starts with the verb; das is the subject and the digit string is the Rest. Answered with Nein. Hier ist null – drei – drei – neun.

4 · Wie viele? (how many?) — the shortest W-question
Wie viele?W-Wort · question word

Wie viele? (How many?) from Dialog 2 is a W-question stripped down to just the question word — no verb, no subject needed, because the answer is a bare number: Sechzehn.

5 · eins counts, ein- attaches — the object slot
Einen MomentAkkusativ · fixed phrasebitte!Rest

eins is used for counting or when 1 stands alone (eins, zwei, drei …); before a noun, use the correctly inflected form of ein- (the full pattern is in Lektion 20/21). Here, masculine Moment is accusative and therefore takes einen: Einen Moment, bitte! — never Eins Moment.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • z = ts; s = z, z = ts (the sound swap): picture a German cat: ca-ts — every z in this Lektion is a cat: zwei, zehn, zwanzig. The two letters swapped jobs: sieben buzzes like a bee, zwei clicks like a clock.
  • -zehn is -teen: thirteen ↔ dreizehn. Same idea, same slot, different clothes — seven of the twenty-one words come free once you see the pattern.
  • sechs und sieben auf Diät (sechs and sieben on a diet): both lose weight before -zehn: sech(s)zehn, sieb(en)zehn — and they diet again as sechzig, siebzig in Lektion 4.
  • elf und zwölf sind Rebellen (elf and zwölf are rebels): English refused to say oneteen and twoteen too — German rebelled at exactly the same two numbers.
  • zwo rettet den Anruf (zwo saves the phone call): zwei and drei rhyme, so a bad line confuses them. Two → zwo → no confusion. Recognise it; you do not need to use it yourself yet.
  • -ig = -ikh: in standard German, the final g goes soft and breathy, like the end of ich — zwanz-ig → zwan-ts-ikh. This also applies to the numbers ending in -zig in Lektion 4 (dreißig, vierzig …).
  • fünf braucht einen Pfiff (fünf needs a whistle): round your lips as if to whistle, then say "eenf". No pucker, no fünf.
  • Handy ist ein deutsches Wort (Handy is a German word); Nummer beschriftet, Zahl zählt (Nummer labels, Zahl counts): Handy looks English but is a genuine German word for a mobile phone — nobody in English uses it that way. A Nummer identifies something (phone, house, room); a Zahl measures a quantity. Your phone has a Nummer, never a Zahl. The full ein-pattern behind Einen Moment, bitte! is taught in Lektion 20/21 — here you only need the fixed phrase.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • sechszehn → sechzehn — sechs drops its s — say it fast and you hear why.
  • siebenzehn → siebzehn — sieben drops its en.
  • "zvai" for zwei → TSV-EYE — German z is always ts.
  • "tsvan-tsig" → TSVAN-tsikh — in standard German, final -ig is said -ikh.
  • zwolf / funf → zwölf / fünf — the umlaut is part of the spelling, not decoration.
  • "sekhs" for sechs → ZEKS — chs = ks, and the s at the start buzzes.
  • Eins Moment, bitte! → Einen Moment, bitte! — eins counts or stands alone; before a noun you need the correctly inflected form of ein-.
  • Phone: "dreiunddreißig" for 33 → drei – drei — the clarity-first pattern in this lesson reads phone-number digits one at a time.
  • Meine Zahl ist 0176… → Meine Nummer ist … — a phone number is a Nummer, not a Zahl.
  • Eins, Zwei, Drei → eins, zwei, drei — counting words are not nouns, so no capital letter.
4

Zahlen 21–100 (Numbers 21–100)

One strange new idea: German says the units before the tens. einundzwanzig is literally one-and-twenty. Everything else here you already know from Lektion 3.

Die zwei Regeln (the two rules that carry this Lektion)

1 · Einheit zuerst (the unit comes first)

German says the unit before the ten: einundzwanzig is literally one-and-twenty, and vierundachtzig is 84. You write left to right, but you say the last digit first. English used to do this too — “four and twenty blackbirds” — and Urdu still does: اکیس = اک + یس. The trap runs the other way when you listen: hear siebenundvierzig and the hand wants to write 74. It is 47.

2 · 15 Wörter, nicht 101 (15 words, not 101)

You do not memorise a hundred words. This lesson's mnemonic uses 15 anchors: null…neun (10), zehn, elf, zwölf (3), plus dreißig and hundert; keep the familiar zwanzig from Lektion 3 alongside them. Then three recipes generate the rest — +zehn for 13–19, +zig for the tens, and unit + und + ten for everything between. Two diet rules finish it: sechs → sech- and sieben → sieb-, but only before -zehn and -zig, never before und.

Zahlen 0–100 (numbers 0–100)

Read each number, say it in German out loud, then check the word beside it. The compounds make the unit-first pattern visible; the diagram below shows the change of direction.

0 null 1 eins 2 zwei 3 drei 4 vier 5 fünf 6 sechs 7 sieben 8 acht 9 neun 10 zehn 11 elf 12 zwölf 13 dreizehn 14 vierzehn 15 fünfzehn 16 sechzehn 17 siebzehn 18 achtzehn 19 neunzehn 20 zwanzig 21 einundzwanzig 22 zweiundzwanzig 23 dreiundzwanzig 24 vierundzwanzig 25 fünfundzwanzig 26 sechsundzwanzig 27 siebenundzwanzig 28 achtundzwanzig 29 neunundzwanzig 30 dreißig 31 einunddreißig 32 zweiunddreißig 33 dreiunddreißig 34 vierunddreißig 35 fünfunddreißig 36 sechsunddreißig 37 siebenunddreißig 38 achtunddreißig 39 neununddreißig 40 vierzig 41 einundvierzig 42 zweiundvierzig 43 dreiundvierzig 44 vierundvierzig 45 fünfundvierzig 46 sechsundvierzig 47 siebenundvierzig 48 achtundvierzig 49 neunundvierzig 50 fünfzig 51 einundfünfzig 52 zweiundfünfzig 53 dreiundfünfzig 54 vierundfünfzig 55 fünfundfünfzig 56 sechsundfünfzig 57 siebenundfünfzig 58 achtundfünfzig 59 neunundfünfzig 60 sechzig 61 einundsechzig 62 zweiundsechzig 63 dreiundsechzig 64 vierundsechzig 65 fünfundsechzig 66 sechsundsechzig 67 siebenundsechzig 68 achtundsechzig 69 neunundsechzig 70 siebzig 71 einundsiebzig 72 zweiundsiebzig 73 dreiundsiebzig 74 vierundsiebzig 75 fünfundsiebzig 76 sechsundsiebzig 77 siebenundsiebzig 78 achtundsiebzig 79 neunundsiebzig 80 achtzig 81 einundachtzig 82 zweiundachtzig 83 dreiundachtzig 84 vierundachtzig 85 fünfundachtzig 86 sechsundachtzig 87 siebenundachtzig 88 achtundachtzig 89 neunundachtzig 90 neunzig 91 einundneunzig 92 zweiundneunzig 93 dreiundneunzig 94 vierundneunzig 95 fünfundneunzig 96 sechsundneunzig 97 siebenundneunzig 98 achtundneunzig 99 neunundneunzig 100 hundert

The 15 bold forms are the lesson's memory anchors. Keep zwanzig, the familiar 20-form from Lektion 3, alongside them; then three recipes (+zehn, +zig, unit+und+ten) account for the remaining forms. The tens are zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig and neunzig.

Stolperfallen (pitfalls)

  • 3️⃣dreißigthirty /ˈdʁaɪ̯sɪç/ · DR-EYE-ssikh — In the spelling standard used here, this is the only ten with ß instead of z. Swiss Standard German uses ss because it does not use ß.
  • 6️⃣sechzigsixty /ˈzɛçtsɪç/ · ZEKH-tsikh — sechs drops its s again — same rule as sechzehn.
  • 7️⃣siebzigseventy /ˈziːptsɪç/ · ZEEP-tsikh — sieben drops its en again — same rule as siebzehn.
  • 4️⃣vierzigforty /ˈfɪʁtsɪç/ · FEER-tsikh — Short i, exactly like vierzehn — vier alone is long (FEE-uh).

Zusammengesetzte Zahlen — Muster (compound numbers — the pattern)

  • 2️⃣1️⃣einundzwanzigtwenty-one /ˈaɪ̯nʊntˌtsvantsɪç/ · EYE-n-unt-TSVAN-tsikh — Unit first: one-and-twenty. Before und in compound tens, use ein-, never eins-.
  • 2️⃣6️⃣sechsundzwanzigtwenty-six /ˈzɛksʊntˌtsvantsɪç/ · ZEKS-unt-TSVAN-tsikh — Full sechs here! It only shortens before -zehn and -zig, never before und.
  • 2️⃣7️⃣siebenundzwanzigtwenty-seven /ˈziːbn̩ʊntˌtsvantsɪç/ · ZEE-bn-unt-TSVAN-tsikh — Full sieben here, for the same reason.
  • 7️⃣4️⃣vierundsiebzigseventy-four /ˈfiːɐ̯ʊntˌziːptsɪç/ · FEE-uh-unt-ZEEP-tsikh — You write 7-4, you say four-and-seventy. Read the last digit first.
  • 9️⃣9️⃣neunundneunzigninety-nine /ˈnɔɪ̯nʊntˌnɔɪ̯ntsɪç/ · NOYN-unt-NOYN-tsikh — Nine-and-ninety. Easy to mishear as neunzig — read the digits if in doubt.
  • 💯einhundertone hundred /ˈaɪ̯nˈhʊndɐt/ · EYE-n-HUN-duht — Both hundert and einhundert are correct; hundert is common in speech, while einhundert states the one explicitly.

Nach dem Alter fragen (asking someone's age)

  • 🎂Wie alt sind Sie?How old are you? (Sie) /viː ˈalt zɪnt ziː/ · vee alt zint zee — alt = old. This is NOT “how are you” — that is Wie geht es Ihnen? in Lektion 8.
  • 🎈Wie alt bist du?How old are you? (du) /viː ˈalt bɪst duː/ · vee alt bist doo — du, not due. sind → Sie, bist → du: your first two forms of the verb sein.
  • 🎉Ich bin sechzehn Jahre alt.I am sixteen years old. /ɪç bɪn ˈzɛçtseːn ˈjaːʁə alt/ · ikh bin ZEKH-tsayn YAH-ruh alt — Verb bin in slot 2, alt at the very end. You may also just say Ich bin sechzehn.
  • 👶Ich bin ein Jahr alt.I am one year old. /ɪç bɪn aɪ̯n ˈjaːɐ̯ alt/ · ikh bin EYE-n yahr alt — Exactly one year takes the singular Jahr; two and up take Jahre.

Die Regeln als Karten (the rules, as flashcards)

  • 🔁Einheit zuerstunit before ten: 4 + und + 80 — vierundachtzig = 84. English once did this too — “four and twenty blackbirds”. Urdu does it as well: اک+یس.
  • 🧠15 Wörter, nicht 101memorise 15 anchors, generate the rest — 0–9, zehn/elf/zwölf, dreißig and hundert, with zwanzig already known from Lektion 3. Then three recipes: +zehn, +zig, unit+und+ten.
  • ✂️Diät vor zsechs → sech-, sieben → sieb- before -zehn and -zig — sechzehn, sechzig, siebzehn, siebzig — but sechsundzwanzig, siebenundzwanzig keep the full word.
  • 🧍Ich bin … alt, nicht ich habeGerman uses sein for age, like English — Never Ich habe sechzehn Jahre. Urdu says “my age is”, German says “I am”.

Dialoge (dialogues)

Dialog 1 · Wie alt bist du? (How old are you? · two classmates · du)
👧 Lena
Hallo! Wie alt bist du?Hi! How old are you?
🧑 Max
Ich bin siebzehn. Und du?I'm seventeen. And you?
👧 Lena
Ich bin sechzehn Jahre alt.I am sixteen years old.
🧑 Max
Ah, sechzehn!Ah, sixteen!
👧 Lena
Ja. Tschüs!Yes. Bye!
🧑 Max
Tschüs!Bye!

Max drops Jahre alt, Lena keeps it — both are correct. Note siebzehn (shortened) but siebenundzwanzig for 27: the diet only happens before -zehn and -zig.

Dialog 2 · Im Kurs (in the class · Sie)
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Guten Morgen! Wie alt sind Sie?Good morning! How old are you?
🧔 Herr Khan
Ich bin dreiundvierzig Jahre alt.I am forty-three years old.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Wie bitte? Noch einmal, bitte!Pardon? Once again, please!
🧔 Herr Khan
Dreiundvierzig. Vier – drei.Forty-three. Four – three.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Danke schön!Thank you kindly!
🧔 Herr Khan
Bitte!You're welcome!

When the number does not land, he reads the digits — the Lektion 3 habit. Notice the mismatch: he SAYS drei-und-vierzig (3-and-40) but SPELLS vier – drei (4, 3).

Dialog 3 · Die Hausnummer (the house number)
🚕 Taxifahrer
Guten Abend! Wohin?Good evening! Where to?
👵 Frau Ott
Bahnhofstraße achtundsechzig, bitte.Bahnhofstraße 68, please.
🚕 Taxifahrer
Achtundsechzig?Sixty-eight?
👵 Frau Ott
Ja. Sechs – acht.Yes. Six – eight.
🚕 Taxifahrer
Gut!Good!
👵 Frau Ott
Danke!Thanks!

achtundsechzig is 8-and-60, but the digits are 6 – 8. That mismatch is the whole Lektion. Wohin? and Straße are recognise-only.

Dialog 4 · Der Preis (the price)
🧑‍💼 Verkäufer
Das macht neunundneunzig Euro.That comes to 99 euros.
🙋 Kunde
Wie bitte? Neunzig?Pardon? Ninety?
🧑‍💼 Verkäufer
Nein — neunundneunzig. Neun – neun.No — ninety-nine. Nine – nine.
🙋 Kunde
Ah! Kein Problem.Ah! No problem.
🧑‍💼 Verkäufer
Danke schön! Schönen Tag noch!Thank you kindly! Have a nice rest of the day!
🙋 Kunde
Danke, gleichfalls!Thanks, same to you!

neunzig and neunundneunzig sound alike in a noisy shop, so the digits settle it. The closing pair comes straight from Lektion 1.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Nach dem Alter fragen — informell (asking age, informal)
Wie altW-Wort + Adjektiv · question word + adjectivebistsein · verb, position 2du?Subjekt · subject, informal

Wie alt bist du? is not Wie geht's? (how are you?) — alt means "old", and the two words wie + alt travel together as one question chunk before the verb. du is for one person you know informally.

2 · Nach dem Alter fragen — formell (asking age, formal)
Wie altW-Wort + Adjektiv · question word + adjectivesindsein · verb, position 2Sie?Subjekt · subject, formal, capital S

Same chunk, different subject: Wie alt sind Sie? Only the verb form and the pronoun change — bist → sind, du → Sie — nothing else in the sentence moves.

3 · Antworten mit sein: Jahr oder Jahre? (answering with sein: year or years?)
IchSubjekt · subjectbinsein · verb, position 2ein Jahr alt.exactly 1 · year, singularsechzehn Jahre alt.2+ · years, plural

Age always uses sein, never haben — ich bin, like English "I am". alt sits at the very end, after the number. Exactly one year is the singular Jahr; two and up switch to Jahre.

4 · Kurz antworten und zurückfragen (answering briefly and asking back)
IchSubjekt · subjectbinsein · verbsiebzehn.Jahre alt weggelassen · years old omittedUnd du?reciprocal question

In speech Jahre alt is often dropped — Ich bin siebzehn is completely normal, as in Dialog 1. Bounce the question back with Und du? (informal) or Und Sie? (formal); a full new question is also correct but is not needed.

5 · Ein Preis ist ein Objekt (a price is an object)
DasSubjekt · subjectmachtVerb · verb, position 2neunundneunzig Euro.Akkusativ · accusative, the amount

Das macht … ("that comes to …") is how prices are given; the number + noun sits in the object slot. For the accusative pattern, see Lektion 19. When a number is hard to catch — neunzig vs neunundneunzig, or an address like achtundsechzig — Germans read the digits one by one to confirm: Vier – drei, Sechs – acht, Neun – neun, exactly as in Dialogs 2, 3 and 4.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • “Four and twenty blackbirds”: the English nursery rhyme is 24 said the German way — English used to count unit-first too, then dropped it; German never did. Urdu still does it as well: = اک (one) + یس (twenty) — einundzwanzig already matches how you would count in Urdu.
  • Letzte Ziffer zuerst (last digit first): for 74, jump to the 4 first, say vier, then und, then siebzig. Train the eye-jump, not the word.
  • eins verliert sein s (eins loses its s before und): alone it is eins; before und in 21, 31 … 91 it becomes ein-: einundzwanzig, never "einsundzwanzig".
  • dreißig ist der Rebell (thirty is the rebel): in the spelling standard used here, it is the only ten with ß. Picture a big ß sitting on the 30. Swiss Standard German instead writes dreissig because it does not use ß.
  • Diät nur vor z (diet only before z): sechs and sieben slim down only before -zehn and -zig — sechzig, siebzig — and eat normally before und: sechsundzwanzig, siebenundzwanzig.
  • -ig = -ikh: every multiple of ten from zwanzig to neunzig ends breathy — vierzikh, achtzikh, neunzikh — in the standard pronunciation taught here, never with the hard g of English "pig".
  • Ein Wort, egal wie lang (one word, however long): written-out German cardinal numbers below one million form one word. Write vierundsiebzig, not "vier und siebzig"; English normally writes seventy-four with a hyphen.
  • Ich bin … alt, nicht ich habe (I am … old, not I have): you ARE your age in German, exactly as in English, never "ich habe". And do not confuse the question with wellbeing: Wie geht es Ihnen? (how are you?) is a different question, from Lektion 8.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • zwanzigeins (for 21) → einundzwanzig — Unit first, then und, then the ten.
  • einsundzwanzig → einundzwanzig — Before und in compound tens, eins drops its s.
  • dreizig → dreißig — The only ten with ß. Learn it as a picture.
  • sechsundsechszig → sechsundsechzig — Full sechs before und; shortened sech- before -zig.
  • siebenzig → siebzig — sieben drops its en before -zig.
  • vier und siebzig → vierundsiebzig — One word, always — no spaces inside a number.
  • hearing siebenundvierzig, writing 74 → 47 — The unit is said first. Hear the whole word, then write the last part first.
  • Ich bin zwei Jahr alt. → Ich bin zwei Jahre alt. — Two and up take the plural Jahre.
  • Ich habe sechzehn Jahre. → Ich bin sechzehn Jahre alt. — German uses sein for age, like English — not haben.
  • “Wie alt sind Sie?” = How are you? → = How old are you? — alt = old. How are you? is Wie geht es Ihnen? (Lektion 8).
5

Das Alphabet (the alphabet)

Your notes teach what each letter sounds like. This teaches what each letter is called — which is the part you need to spell your name at a German counter.

Die zwei Regeln (the two that carry this Lektion)

Buchstabenname ≠ Buchstabenklang (letter name ≠ letter sound)

Your notes teach the sound (A wie Apfel). This Lektion adds the name — what you say when you spell aloud. Four pairs trip up English speakers, and they are worth drilling as pairs: A=AH vs E=AY, E=AY vs I=EE, G=GAY vs J=YOT, V=FOW vs W=VAY. On the phone, add wie + Wort to any letter that rhymes — B, D, E, P and T all sound alike down a bad line.

Umlaut und Eszett (umlaut and Eszett)

Ä Ö Ü are not separate basic letters — they are A, O, U with two dots — but the dots change the word: schon (already) vs schön (beautiful). If you cannot type them, write ae, oe, ue; never just drop them. ß is called Eszett, always sounds like a sharp hissed s, and can never start a word. For this sharp s sound, a long vowel or diphthong before it usually takes ß (Fuß, Straße); a short vowel takes ss (Fluss, Kuss).

Buchstabe (the letters)

  • 🔤der Buchstabe / die Buchstabenletter (of the alphabet)
  • 🍎A aAH · “der Apfel / die Äpfel” — apple · English says “ay” — German says AH.
  • 🍌B bBAY · “die Banane / die Bananen” — banana · rhymes with D, E, P, T — use “B wie Banane” on the phone.
  • 🛋️C cTSAY · “die Couch / die Couches” — couch · not “see”. C alone is rare in German; it usually appears in ch and sch.
  • 🇩🇪D dDAY · “Deutschland” — Germany · rhymes with B, E, P, T.
  • 🐘E eAY · “der Elefant / die Elefanten” — elephant · English “ee” is German I. The whole vowel row is shifted.
  • 🐟F fEFF · “der Fisch / die Fische” — fish · the letter name is essentially the same as in English.
  • 🎸G gGAY · “die Gitarre / die Gitarren” — guitar · the letter name begins with a hard g.
  • 🏠H hHAH · “das Haus / die Häuser” — house · not “aitch”. A silent lengthening h can follow a vowel, as in Uhr.
  • 🦔I iEE · “der Igel / die Igel” — hedgehog · English “eye” is German EI. German I is a plain EE.
  • 🥣J jYOT · “der Joghurt / die Joghurts” — yoghurt · German J usually sounds like English Y, while its letter name is YOT.
  • ☕K kKAH · “der Kaffee / die Kaffees” — coffee · unlike English “kay”, German K is KAH.
  • ❤️L lELL · “die Liebe” — love (no usual plural) · the letter name is essentially the same as in English.
  • 👨M mEMM · “der Mann / die Männer” — man · the letter name is essentially the same as in English.
  • 🔩N nENN · “der Nagel / die Nägel” — nail · double n is said Doppel-N when spelling aloud.
  • 🍊O oOH · “die Orange / die Orangen” — orange · close to English O, but without its final w-glide.
  • 🐧P pPAY · “der Pinguin / die Pinguine” — penguin · not “pee”. Rhymes with B, D, E, T.
  • ❓Q qKOO · “das Quiz / die Quiz” — quiz · not “kyoo”. In native German words, q is followed by u.
  • 🔴R rERR · “Rot” — red · a throat r, similar to Urdu غ, is common in Standard German; after a vowel it may weaken toward -uh.
  • ☀️S sESS · “die Sonne / die Sonnen” — sun · at the start of a word before a vowel, s usually buzzes like English z: Sonne = ZON-uh.
  • 🍵T tTAY · “der Tee / die Tees” — tea · not “tee” as in golf — it rhymes with B, D, E, P.
  • ⏰U uOO · “die Uhr / die Uhren” — clock · not “yoo”. A plain oo.
  • 🐦V vFOW · “der Vogel / die Vögel” — bird · the name rhymes with English how. In native words such as Vogel, v is usually pronounced f; some loanwords use a v sound.
  • ☁️W wVAY · “die Wolke / die Wolken” — cloud · not “double-u”. German w normally has the English v sound: Wolke = VOL-kuh.
  • 🎶X xIKS · “das Xylofon / die Xylofone” — xylophone · rare in German. Same sound as English x.
  • 🐃Y yEWP-si-lon · “der Yak / die Yaks” — yak · a whole three-syllable word, not one letter-sound.
  • 🦓Z zTSETT · “das Zebra / die Zebras” — zebra · not “zed”, not “zee”. In native German words, z has the ts sound.
  • 🐻Ä äEH · “der Bär / die Bären” — bear · say the sound itself. It is A with an Umlaut — not a separate basic letter.
  • 🛢️Ö öOE · “das Öl / die Öle” — oil · say the sound itself: “ay” with rounded lips, no r in it.
  • 5️⃣Ü üEW · “fünf” — five · say the sound itself: “ee” with tightly rounded lips.
  • 🦶ßess-TSETT · “der Fuß / die Füße” — foot · called Eszett or scharfes S. Always a sharp hissed s, and it can never start a word.

Buchstabieren (spelling aloud)

  • ❓Wie schreibt man das?vee SHR-EYE-pt man das · How do you write that? · the everyday way to ask for a spelling.
  • 🔤Buchstabieren Sie, bitte!BOOKH-shtah-BEE-rn zee, BIT-uh · /ˌbuːxʃtaˈbiːʁən ziː ˈbɪtə/ · formell (formal) Please spell it! · another Sie-command — verb first, Sie second, bitte to soften. Same shape as Wiederholen Sie!
  • 🍎A wie ApfelAH vee AP-fl · A as in Apfel · the repair move that saves you on the phone, because B, D, E, P and T all rhyme.
  • 🔠großes A / kleines aGROH-sess AH / KL-EYE-ness AH · capital A / small a · needed whenever a name starts with a capital or contains one. groß itself contains a ß.
  • 🔁Doppel-NDOP-l ENN · double N · Schmitt = S – C – H – M – I – Doppel-T.

Regel (rule)

  • ✏️Ä Ö Ü sind keine neuen BuchstabenUmlauts are A, O, U with two dots — not separate basic letters · the dots change the word: schon (already) vs schön (beautiful). Cannot type them? Write ae, oe, ue.
  • ⚖️ß oder ss?For the sharp s sound: long vowel or diphthong → ß · short vowel → ss · Fuß, Straße, weiß (long) — Fluss, Kuss, muss (short). Switzerland always writes ss.
  • ⚠️Die vier FallenA/E, E/I, G/J, V/W · German A=AH, E=AY, I=EE — shifted from English. J=YOT, V=FOW, W=VAY. Drill them as pairs.

Dialog 1 — Im Hotel (at the hotel)

🛎️ Rezeption
Guten Abend! Wie ist Ihr Familienname?Good evening! What is your surname?
🙋 Gast
Ahmad.Ahmad.
🛎️ Rezeption
Wie schreibt man das?How do you write that?
🙋 Gast
A – H – M – A – D.A-H-M-A-D.
🛎️ Rezeption
Noch einmal, bitte! Langsam.Once again, please! Slowly.
🙋 Gast
A wie Apfel – H wie Haus – M wie Mann – A – D wie Deutschland.A as in Apfel, H as in Haus, M as in Mann, A, D as in Deutschland.
🛎️ Rezeption
Danke schön! Zimmer vierundzwanzig.Thank you kindly! Room twenty-four.
🙋 Gast
Vielen Dank!Thank you very much!

📌 The first attempt fails, so the guest switches to wie + Wort. That is the normal repair move, not bad German. The room number is vierundzwanzig — unit first, straight from Lektion 4.

Dialog 2 — Der Umlaut (the umlaut)

🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Wie heißen Sie mit Familiennamen?What is your surname?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Öztürk
Öztürk.Öztürk.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Buchstabieren Sie, bitte!Please spell it!
🙋‍♂️ Herr Öztürk
Großes Ö – Z – T – Ü – R – K.Capital Ö – Z – T – Ü – R – K.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Ö wie Öl?Ö as in Öl?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Öztürk
Ja, genau. Ö wie Öl.Yes, exactly. Ö as in Öl.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Danke!Thanks!

📌 großes Ö tells her it is a capital. genau (exactly) is a bonus word Germans use constantly — recognise it. Wie heißen Sie …? belongs to Lektion 7; recognise-only here.

Dialog 3 — V oder W? (on the telephone)

☎️ Frau Ott
Wie ist Ihr Name?What is your name?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Weber
Weber.Weber.
☎️ Frau Ott
Mit V oder mit W?With V or with W?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Weber
Mit W — W wie Wolke.With W — W as in Wolke.
☎️ Frau Ott
Ah! W – E – B – E – R.Ah! W-E-B-E-R.
🙋‍♂️ Herr Weber
Genau. Danke!Exactly. Thanks!
☎️ Frau Ott
Bitte. Auf Wiederhören!You're welcome. Goodbye!

📌 This is THE German phone question, because V (FOW) and W (VAY) are the pair English speakers mix up most. Auf Wiederhören, not Auf Wiedersehen, because it is a phone call.

Dialog 4 — Straße oder Strasse? (ß or ss?)

👨‍🏫 Lehrer
Wie schreibt man „Fuß“?How do you write “Fuß”?
🙋‍♀️ Sara
F – U – Eszett.F – U – Eszett.
👨‍🏫 Lehrer
Sehr gut! Und „Fluss“?Very good! And “Fluss”?
🙋‍♀️ Sara
F – L – U – Doppel-S.F – L – U – double S.
👨‍🏫 Lehrer
Genau! Fuß mit Eszett, Fluss mit Doppel-S.Exactly! Fuß with ß, Fluss with ss.
🙋‍♀️ Sara
Danke!Thanks!

📌 The long u in Fuß takes ß; the short u in Fluss takes ss. That is the whole rule. sehr gut is recognise-only — it comes back properly in Lektion 8.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau beim Buchstabieren (sentence structure for spelling)

1 · Wie schreibt man das? (How do you write that?) — a W-question with man
WieW-Wort · question wordschreibtVerb · position 2manSubjekt · one, youdas?Objekt · that

man is the general "one / you / people", so Wie schreibt man das? is literally "How does one write that?" — the everyday request for a spelling, used to open Dialog 1. The W-word takes position 1, the verb stays glued to position 2, and the subject follows.

2 · Buchstabieren Sie, bitte! (Please spell it!) — the formal imperative
BuchstabierenVerb · position 1SieSubjekt · formal youbitte!softener

A polite instruction to a stranger puts the verb first and Sie right after it, exactly like Wiederholen Sie! (Lektion 8). Adding bitte turns a command into a request — the shape the Beamtin uses in Dialog 2.

3 · Wie ist Ihr Familienname? (What is your surname?) — sein (to be) + formal possessive
WieW-Wort · question wordistVerb · position 2Ihr Familienname?Subjekt · formal possessive

The receptionist's opener from Dialog 1: W-word, then sein in position 2, then the subject. Ihr capitalised is the formal possessive (Lektion 24) — lowercase ihr would mean "her/their". Wie heißen Sie? (Dialog 2) asks the same thing a different way and belongs properly to Lektion 7.

4 · Buchstabe (letter) + wie (as in) + Beispielwort (example word) — the repair formula
ABuchstabe · letterwieas, likeApfelBeispielwort · example word

Not a full sentence but a fixed three-piece chunk, repeated for every letter that might be misheard: A wie Apfel, H wie Haus, M wie Mann, D wie Deutschland (Dialog 1), Ö wie Öl (Dialog 2), W wie Wolke (Dialog 3). It exists because B, D, E, P, T all rhyme down a bad phone line.

5 · Mit V oder mit W? (With V or W?) — the confusable-letter check
Mit Vmit · with + Buchstabe · letteroderormit W?mit · with + Buchstabe · letter

A short fragment, not a full clause — mit (with) plus the bare letter, used specifically for the one pair German speakers themselves cannot always tell apart by ear: V (FOW) and W (VAY). Frau Ott asks this after hearing Herr Weber's surname.

6 · Scharfes s: lang → ß, kurz → ss (sharp s: long → ß, short → ss) — a spelling rule, not a verb form
Fußlanger Vokal · long vowel → ßFlusskurzer Vokal · short vowel → ss

No subject or verb here — this chip pair shows the spelling of the sharp s sound from Dialog 4: the long u in Fuß is followed by ß; the short u in Fluss is followed by ss. This contrast applies when the consonant is a sharp, voiceless s sound.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • A-E-I slide one step: German A = ah, E = ay, I = ee. English A resembles German E, and English E resembles German I; learn German A separately as AH.
  • J is Y: Joghurt is "yoghurt". Since J already does Y's job in German, the letter needed its own name: YOT.
  • V and W follow their usual native-word sounds: V is called FOW (rhymes with English how) and is usually f in native words such as Vogel. W is called VAY and normally has the English v sound, as in Wolke (VOL-kuh).
  • Z wie Zebra (Z as in Zebra): a German zebra is a "TSebra". In native German words, Z normally has a ts sound — its letter name is TSETT, not "zed" or "zee".
  • Es-Zett (the names of S + Z): the name Eszett combines Es and Zett. Historically, ß developed from ligatures involving a long s with s or z. It is also called scharfes S (sharp S): hissing like the s of hiss, never buzzing like the s of rose.
  • For sharp s: long → ß, short → ss: after a long vowel or diphthong, write ß (Fuß); after a short vowel, write ss (Fluss).
  • groß (large) has a ß in it: the spelling term großes A means "capital A", and groß itself contains an Eszett.
  • ae, oe, ue instead of nothing: no German keyboard? In ordinary text, write Baer, schoen, fuer rather than dropping the dots. Preserve the official spelling of a person's name whenever possible.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • E said as "ee" → AY — German E = ay. English "ee" is the German letter I.
  • I said as "eye" → EE — German I = ee. English "eye" is the German diphthong ei.
  • J said as "jay" → YOT — German J sounds like English Y.
  • W said as "double-u" → VAY — German W says v, and its name follows the sound.
  • V said as "vee" → FOW — the letter name begins with f and rhymes with how; v is also usually pronounced f in native German words.
  • Z said as "zed" → TSETT — in native German words, Z normally has the ts sound.
  • Bar for Bär → Bär — dropping the umlaut changes the word — or destroys it.
  • fur for für → für (or fuer) — if you cannot type ü, write ue — never nothing.
  • ß at the start of a word → impossible — ß never begins a German word.
  • Fluß → Fluss — for the sharp s sound, a short vowel takes ss; a long vowel or diphthong takes ß.
6

Sich vorstellen (Introducing yourself)
